The first thing the lighthouse keeper did after retiring was buy curtains.

For forty-three years, he had slept in rooms that could never be properly dark. Light climbed the walls, crossed the ceiling, and moved on. Every twelve seconds, the world looked in.

Now he lived above a bakery, forty miles from the sea.

The curtains were green. He closed them at six in the evening, though it was summer and the street was still bright, and stood in the room to see whether they worked.

They did.

For several weeks, he slept badly.

He missed the machinery’s steady turning. He missed the stairs, which had made his knees hurt but had also settled the question of what his knees were for. Most of all, he missed having one necessary thing to do.

Downstairs, the baker began work at four.

There were small noises: a door catching, trays touching, the soft, heavy arrival of flour. The keeper learned them without intending to. After a while, he could tell whether she was making the dark rye or the little round loaves before the smell reached him.

One morning, the noises stopped.

He lay awake until half past four. Then he dressed and went downstairs.

The baker was sitting on an overturned bucket with her hand wrapped in a towel.

“Cut myself,” she said. “Nothing serious. But I can’t knead.”

He looked at the pale dough waiting on the bench.

“I don’t know how.”

“I have one good hand. I can point.”

So he washed, rolled up his sleeves, and began.

He was too rough at first. Then too careful.

“It isn’t an injured bird,” she told him.

By six, his shoulders ached. By seven, the first customers had come in, bringing wet umbrellas and the day’s complaints.

He carried trays. He gave someone the wrong change. He learned that the smallest loaf belonged to a woman who would insist every morning that it had got smaller.

The baker’s hand healed.

He kept coming down.

Months later, a former colleague visited and asked whether he missed the lighthouse.

They sat at the kitchen table eating bread that the keeper had made. He considered the question.

“Yes,” he said.

His colleague waited.

Outside, the bakery sign creaked in the wind. The keeper brushed some crumbs together with the side of his hand.

“But I have to get up early tomorrow.”

At six, he closed the green curtains.
